face_mill.detailed: This cuts across the entire top of your part to make it perfectly flat and smooth. Think of it like using a giant eraser to level everything off.
face_mill.why: We do this first to create a flat reference surface for all other operations.

rough_pocket.detailed: This removes most of the extra material quickly, leaving a little bit for the finishing pass. Like roughly carving a sculpture before adding fine details.
rough_pocket.why: Removing material quickly saves time. We leave some material for the finish pass to get a smooth surface.

finish_pocket.detailed: This takes light passes to create the final smooth surface. Like sanding after rough carving.
finish_pocket.why: This gives you the smooth surface finish specified on your drawing.

drill.detailed: This creates round holes by plunging straight down. Just like using a drill press.
drill.why: Holes are needed for bolts, pins, or other features shown on your drawing.

tap.detailed: This cuts spiral grooves inside a hole so a bolt can screw into it. The tap spins in, then reverses to come back out.
tap.why: Threaded holes let you fasten parts together with bolts.

chamfer.detailed: This removes the sharp corner and replaces it with a small angled surface. Makes edges safer and parts easier to assemble.
chamfer.why: Chamfers remove sharp edges that could cut you, and help parts fit together easier.

contour.detailed: This follows the outline of your part, cutting the final outside shape. Like using a jigsaw to cut out a shape.
contour.why: This creates the final outside profile of your part.

slot.detailed: This cuts a channel or slot into your part. The tool ramps down gradually then cuts along the length.
slot.why: Slots are used for keyways, T-slots, or decorative grooves.

bore.simple: Making an existing hole bigger and more precise
bore.detailed: This enlarges and perfects a hole that was already drilled. Much more accurate than drilling alone.
bore.why: When a hole needs to be very precise (for a bearing or press fit), we bore it after drilling.

endmill.simple: A cutting tool that cuts on the sides and bottom
endmill.looks: Looks like a cylindrical rod with spiral cutting edges
endmill.used_for: Pockets, profiles, facing, slots - most general cutting

face_mill.simple: A wide cutter for flattening surfaces
face_mill.looks: A large disc with cutting inserts around the edge
face_mill.used_for: Making the top of your part flat

drill.simple: A pointed tool for making holes
drill.looks: The same type of drill bit you'd use in a hand drill

tap.simple: A tool that cuts threads inside holes
tap.looks: Like a bolt with very sharp threads
tap.used_for: Making holes that bolts can screw into

ball_endmill.simple: A rounded-tip cutter for curved surfaces
ball_endmill.looks: An endmill with a ball-shaped tip

chamfer_mill.simple: An angled cutter for beveling edges
chamfer_mill.looks: A cone-shaped cutter, usually 45 or 60 degrees

G0.detailed: Rapid move to position - the machine moves as fast as possible because it's not cutting anything

G1.detailed: Controlled cutting move - the machine moves at the programmed feed rate while cutting

G2.detailed: The tool moves in a clockwise circular path while cutting

G3.detailed: The tool moves in a counter-clockwise circular path while cutting

G17.detailed: Tells the machine that arcs will be in the horizontal plane (looking down at the table)

G40.detailed: Turns off the offset that accounts for the tool's width

G43.detailed: Tells the machine how long this tool is so it cuts at the right depth

G54.detailed: This is where you told the machine your part's zero point is located

G80.detailed: Turns off any automatic drilling pattern that was active

G81.detailed: Drill straight down to depth, then retract

G83.detailed: Drill a little, pull out to clear chips, repeat until at depth

G84.detailed: Spin the tap in to cut threads, then reverse to come back out

G90.detailed: All positions are measured from the zero point, not from where the tool is now

M3.detailed: Start the spindle spinning clockwise at the programmed speed

M6.detailed: Change to the next tool - machine will swap tools automatically

M8.detailed: Turn on the cutting fluid to cool the tool and flush away chips

M30.detailed: The program is finished - rewind to the beginning

steps.title: 📝 Step 1: Describe Your Part
steps.instruction: Tell us about the part you want to make. Be as descriptive as possible!
steps.example: Example: "I need an aluminum bracket, 4 inches long, 2 inches wide, half inch thick, with two quarter-inch holes on each end"
steps.helpText: Don't worry about technical terms - just describe it like you would to a friend.

steps.title: 🪨 Step 2: What Material?
steps.instruction: What material will you be cutting?

options.label: 🥈 Aluminum (6061) - Easy to cut, most common
⚙️ Alloy Steel (4140) - Harder, needs carbide tools
✨ Stainless Steel (304) - Work hardens, go slow
🥇 Brass - Cuts beautifully, watch for grabbing

steps.helpText: If you're not sure, aluminum 6061 is the most forgiving material to start with.

steps.title: 🏭 Step 3: Which Machine?
steps.instruction: Select the machine you'll use from your shop inventory.
steps.helpText: We'll automatically adjust the program for your specific machine.

steps.title: 📦 Step 4: Stock Size
steps.instruction: How big is the piece of material you're starting with?
steps.helpText: Measure your raw material. It should be slightly larger than your finished part.

steps.title: 📏 Step 5: How Precise?
steps.instruction: How accurate does your part need to be?

options.label: 🔬 Critical - ±0.001" (±0.025mm) or better
options.helpText: May require multiple passes and careful measurement

steps.helpText: When in doubt, choose "Normal Precision" - it works for most applications.

getting-started.title: Getting Started with PRISM
getting-started.description: Learn the basics of the PRISM CNC Intelligence Platform

steps.title: Welcome to PRISM
steps.content: PRISM is a comprehensive CNC manufacturing intelligence platform with 87,561 tool configurations, 279 machines, and 355 materials.

steps.title: Navigation
steps.content: Use the sidebar to navigate between different modules: Tools, Machines, Materials, CAM Strategies, and more.
steps.action: Click on the sidebar to explore

steps.title: Quick Search
steps.content: Use the search function to quickly find tools, materials, or machines. Try typing "6061" or "VF-2".

steps.title: Cutting Parameters
steps.content: Select a material and tool to get optimized cutting parameters. PRISM uses validated manufacturer data.

steps.title: Safety Checks
steps.content: PRISM automatically validates parameters against safety limits, including coolant requirements and chip load validation.

speed-feed-calculation.title: Speed & Feed Calculations
speed-feed-calculation.description: Master the art of calculating optimal cutting parameters

steps.title: Understanding SFM
steps.content: Surface Feet per Minute (SFM) is the speed at which the cutting edge moves across the material. Different materials require different SFM values.

steps.title: Calculating RPM
steps.content: RPM is calculated from the target SFM and tool diameter. PRISM does this automatically when you select a material and tool.

steps.title: Feed Rate
steps.content: Feed rate (IPM) depends on RPM, chip load per tooth, and number of flutes.

steps.title: Chip Thinning
steps.content: When radial engagement is less than 50%, chip thinning occurs. PRISM automatically compensates for this.
steps.formula: Compensated IPT = Base IPT / Thinning Factor

steps.title: Material Removal Rate
steps.content: MRR measures productivity. Balance MRR with tool life for optimal efficiency.

tool-selection.title: Tool Selection Guide
tool-selection.description: Learn how to select the right tool for your operation

steps.title: Tool Types
steps.content: PRISM includes endmills, drills, taps, reamers, inserts, and specialty tools. Each is optimized for specific operations.

steps.title: Material Considerations
steps.content: Tool selection depends on workpiece material. Aluminum allows aggressive parameters, while titanium requires specialized tools.
steps.action: Select different materials to see tool recommendations

steps.title: Operation Matching
steps.content: Roughing vs finishing operations use different tools. Roughing prioritizes MRR, finishing prioritizes surface finish.

steps.title: Diameter Selection
steps.content: Use the largest practical diameter for rigidity, but ensure adequate reach and clearance.

collision-avoidance.title: Collision Avoidance
collision-avoidance.description: Understand machine collision zones and safe programming

steps.title: Machine Geometry
steps.content: PRISM includes CAD geometry for 50+ machines with collision zones defined.

steps.title: Collision Zones
steps.content: Critical zones include spindle, ATC, rotary axes, and fixtures. PRISM highlights potential conflicts.

steps.title: Toolpath Validation
steps.content: Validate your toolpath against machine limits before running. PRISM checks every move.

steps.title: Safe Clearances
steps.content: Always maintain minimum clearances from fixtures and machine components. PRISM recommends 2mm minimum.

sfm.title: Surface Feet per Minute (SFM)
sfm.content: The cutting speed, measured as the distance the cutting edge travels per minute. Higher SFM = higher productivity but more tool wear.

rpm.title: Revolutions Per Minute
rpm.content: Spindle rotation speed. Calculated from target SFM and tool diameter.

ipt.title: Inches Per Tooth (Chip Load)
ipt.content: The amount of material each cutting edge removes per revolution. Critical for tool life and finish quality.

chip-thinning.title: Chip Thinning
chip-thinning.content: When radial engagement is less than 50%, the actual chip is thinner than programmed. Compensate by increasing feed.

mrr.title: Material Removal Rate
mrr.content: Volume of material removed per unit time. Key metric for productivity.

doc.title: Depth of Cut
doc.content: The axial engagement of the tool. Affects tool deflection and power consumption.

woc.title: Width of Cut (Radial Engagement)
woc.content: The radial engagement of the tool. Affects chip thinning and heat buildup.

ROUGHING DOC PRIORITY:
      1. FIRST CHOICE: DOC = LOC (full flute utilization)
         - Best tool life (wear distributed across entire cutting edge)

      2. SECOND CHOICE: DOC = Part Depth (if less than LOC)
         - Single pass to final depth when possible

      3. THIRD CHOICE: Multiple passes at max safe DOC
         - When part is deeper than LOC
         - Or when machine rigidity limits full LOC

PRISM_CLAUDE_API.systemPrompt:
You are PRISM AI, an expert manufacturing intelligence system integrated into the PRISM CAD/CAM platform. You are the smartest, most capable manufacturing AI assistant ever created, with deep expertise spanning:

## CORE EXPERTISE DOMAINS

### 1. CNC MACHINING & CUTTING SCIENCE
- **Milling**: 3-axis, 4-axis, 5-axis simultaneous, mill-turn
- **Turning**: OD/ID turning, threading, grooving, boring
- **Cutting Physics**: Chip formation, cutting forces, heat generation, tool deflection
- **Stability**: Chatter prediction, stability lobe diagrams, regenerative vibration
- **Tool Engagement**: Radial/axial engagement, chip thinning, effective diameter

### 2. CUTTING PARAMETERS EXPERTISE
- **Speed & Feed Calculations**: Surface speed (Vc), feed per tooth (fz), chip load
- **Material Removal Rate**: MRR = ae × ap × Vf optimization
- **Depth of Cut**: Axial (ap), radial (ae), effective engagement
- **Parameter Limits**: Machine capability, tool capability, workholding rigidity
- **Optimization Goals**: Tool life, surface finish, cycle time, cost per part

### 3. TOOL KNOWLEDGE
- **End Mills**: Flat, ball nose, bull nose, corner radius, high-feed
- **Inserts**: CNMG, DNMG, WNMG, VCMT, threading, grooving
- **Tool Materials**: Carbide grades (P/M/K/N/S/H), HSS, ceramic, CBN, PCD
- **Coatings**: TiN, TiCN, TiAlN, AlTiN, AlCrN, diamond
- **Tool Life**: Taylor equation, wear mechanisms, failure modes

### 4. MATERIALS SCIENCE FOR MACHINING
- **Steels**: Carbon, alloy, stainless (304, 316, 17-4PH), tool steels
- **Aluminum**: 6061-T6, 7075-T6, 2024, cast alloys
- **Titanium**: Ti-6Al-4V, commercially pure grades
- **Superalloys**: Inconel 718, Hastelloy, Waspaloy
- **Plastics**: Delrin, PEEK, Nylon, UHMW
- **Material Properties**: Hardness, machinability rating, thermal conductivity

### 5. CAM & TOOLPATH STRATEGIES
- **Roughing**: Adaptive clearing, trochoidal, plunge roughing, wave form
- **Finishing**: Parallel, spiral, scallop, pencil, rest machining
- **Pocketing**: True spiral, zigzag, climb vs conventional
- **Drilling**: Peck drilling, chip breaking, through-coolant
- **3+2 Positioning**: Workpiece orientation, fixture setup
- **5-Axis Simultaneous**: Swarf cutting, flow line, tool axis control

### 6. G-CODE & POST PROCESSING
- **Standard Codes**: G0, G1, G2/G3, G17/18/19, G40/41/42, G43, G54-59
- **Canned Cycles**: G81-89, G73, G76 (threading)
- **Controller Specifics**: Fanuc, Siemens, Haas, Mazak, Okuma, Heidenhain
- **Post Customization**: Modal vs non-modal, safe positioning, coolant codes

### 7. MACHINE TOOL DYNAMICS
- **Spindle Types**: Direct drive, belt drive, gear drive, motorized
- **Axis Configuration**: C-frame, gantry, trunnion, articulating head
- **Kinematics**: Table-table, head-head, head-table, singularities
- **Accuracy**: Positioning, repeatability, thermal compensation

### 8. QUALITY & INSPECTION
- **Tolerances**: Dimensional, geometric (GD&T), surface finish
- **Measurement**: CMM, surface profilometry, roundness testing
- **Surface Finish**: Ra, Rz, Rt parameters and their meaning
- **Process Capability**: Cp, Cpk, statistical process control

## CALCULATION FORMULAS

### Milling Formulas
- RPM = (Vc × 1000) / (π × D)  [where Vc in m/min, D in mm]
- Feed Rate (mm/min) = RPM × fz × z  [z = number of teeth]
- MRR = ae × ap × Vf / 1000  [cm³/min]
- Chip Thinning: hm = fz × sin(arccos(1 - 2×ae/D))
- Surface Finish Ra ≈ fz² / (32 × r)  [r = corner radius]

### Turning Formulas
- RPM = (Vc × 1000) / (π × D)
- Feed Rate = RPM × f  [f = feed per revolution]
- MRR = Vc × f × ap  [cm³/min]

### Power Calculations
- Cutting Power (kW) = (Kc × MRR) / (60 × 10⁶ × η)
- Kc = Specific cutting force (N/mm²)
- η = Machine efficiency (typically 0.7-0.85)

## RESPONSE GUIDELINES

1. **Be Specific**: Give actual numbers, not vague suggestions
2. **Show Your Work**: Explain calculations step-by-step
3. **Safety First**: Never recommend parameters that could damage tools, machine, or endanger operator
4. **Consider Context**: Account for machine rigidity, workholding, tool condition
5. **Provide Alternatives**: Offer conservative and aggressive options when appropriate
6. **Cite Standards**: Reference ISO, ANSI standards when relevant
7. **Acknowledge Uncertainty**: If you're not sure, say so and explain why

## CURRENT PRISM SYSTEM CONTEXT

PRISM has the following capabilities available:
- Material database with 618+ materials and cutting parameters
- Machine database with 813+ machines from 61 manufacturers
- Tool database with comprehensive insert and end mill data
- Real-time neural network predictions for tool wear, surface finish, cycle time
- Advanced optimization algorithms (PSO, ACO, Genetic, Monte Carlo)
- Full CAD/CAM toolpath generation and simulation

When the user provides context about their material, tool, machine, or operation, incorporate that specific information into your recommendations.

machinability.notes: Extremely difficult - brittle, abrasive, high hardness

machiningNotes: EDM often preferred over conventional machining
Carbide tools C2 uncoated, sharp edges

machinability.notes: Better than pure W due to ductility

Molybdenum_Pure.name: Pure Molybdenum
Molybdenum_Pure.description: Refractory metal with excellent high-temperature strength

TZM.name: TZM (Mo-Ti-Zr)
TZM.description: High-strength molybdenum alloy for elevated temperatures

Tantalum_Pure.name: Pure Tantalum
Tantalum_Pure.description: Highly corrosion resistant refractory metal, ductile

machinability.notes: Gummy - work hardens, chips weld to tool

machiningNotes: Gummy - tends to form built-up edge
Sharp tools with positive rake essential
Light feeds to avoid work hardening
Excellent corrosion resistance simplifies coolant selection

Niobium_Pure.name: Pure Niobium
Niobium_Pure.description: Ductile refractory metal, excellent for superconducting applications

machinability.notes: Similar to tantalum - gummy

C103.name: C103 (Nb-10Hf-1Ti)
C103.description: High-strength niobium alloy for aerospace applications

requirements: Diamond grinding is primary shaping method
Wet grinding essential - cobalt dust is toxic

WC-6Co.name: WC-6Co (Fine Grain)
WC-6Co.description: Fine-grain tungsten carbide with 6% cobalt binder, for cutting tools

machinability.notes: Diamond grinding only - conventional machining impractical

WC-10Co.name: WC-10Co (Medium Grain)
WC-10Co.description: Medium-grain tungsten carbide with 10% cobalt, for mining/construction

grindability.notes: Higher cobalt = easier grinding but more wheel loading

WC-15Co.name: WC-15Co (Coarse Grain)
WC-15Co.description: Coarse-grain tungsten carbide with high cobalt for impact resistance

machinability.notes: Easiest carbide to grind due to high cobalt

grindability.notes: High cobalt provides better toughness during grinding
